The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

Three concrete, machine-checked witnesses (all produced by a from-scratch FIDE legal-move generator in the script, validated against the published perft values: startpos perft(1..4) = 20/400/8902/197281 and Kiwipete perft(1..3) = 48/2039/97862).

FEN r1bqkbnr/pP3ppp/n3p3/8/8/8/PPPP1PPP/RNBQKBNR w KQkq -. The single White pawn on b7 has exactly 12 legal moves: b7b8=Q/R/B/N, b7xa8=Q/R/B/N (capturing the rook), b7xc8=Q/R/B/N (capturing the bishop). Claim says pawn_moves <= 3; here pawn_moves = 12 > 3.

The White pawn on its home square b2 has 4 legal moves: b3, b4, bxa3 (bishop), bxc3 (knight). Claim says <= 3; here 4 > 3.

The 132 total allocates exactly one queen (1*28); promotion makes that premise false in reachable play, and a side may own up to 9 queens.

The generator counts exactly 218 legal moves. Claim says total <= 132; here 218 > 132. A sparser variant 8/3Q4/1Q4Q1/4Q3/2Q4Q/Q4Q2/pp6/k4K2 w - - (8 White queens + Kf1 vs Ka1, pawns a2,b2) gives exactly 175 > 132. ## What it kills

The flagged claim: **The proof's per-position branching bound: "For a pawn there are at most 3 moves ... for a total of 132 possible moves" per position, which underlies the claimed upper bound 132^4851 on the number of chess games.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> For a pawn there are at most 3 moves, 14 for a rook, 8 for a knight, 14 for a bishop, 28 for a queen and 8 for a king, for a total of 132 possible moves.

Context of the original problem:

> What is the computational complexity of "solving" chess?
> 
> The basic idea of backwards induction is to start with all the possible final positions of a game in which player X wins. So for chess, look at all the ways White can checkmate Black. Now work backwards to all the possible moves/positions that would allow White to move in to one of those positions. If White ever found herself in such a position she could win by moving to the relevant checkmating move. Now we work backwards another step and so on. Eventually we get back to all the possible first moves White could make. The point is, once we've done this, we know that we have White's best response to any move Black makes.
> 
> Recently (last five years or so) Checkers was "solved" in this way. Obviously Noughts and Crosses (what the colonials might call "Tic-Tac-Toe") has been solved for ages. At the very least since this [xkcd][1] but  [...]

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The sentence asserts a per-position branching bound obtained by multiplying per-piece move maxima by the INITIAL piece multiset (8 pawns, 2 rooks, 2 knights, 2 bishops, 1 queen, 1 king): 8*3 + 2*14 + 2*8 + 2*14 + 1*28 + 1*8 = 132. Both the per-piece pawn factor and the multiset are false.

(1) Per-pawn factor. Exhaustive enumeration over 2 colours x 48 legal pawn squares x 3^4 = 81 blocker patterns of the four squares a pawn can ever move to (5760 states, all distinct-outcome cases covered) gives a maximum of 12 pawn moves when promotion choices are counted as distinct moves, and 4 when all four promotions are collapsed into one move. Both exceed 3. A pawn on rank 2 with two capturable enemy men on its capture diagonals has push + double push + 2 captures = 4 moves; a pawn on rank 7 with two capturable men on rank 8 has 3 destinations x 4 promotion pieces = 12 moves. The 4-move and 12-move cases both occur in positions verified reachable from the standard array in 4-5 moves. For an argument that counts GAMES as sequences of moves (which is what 132^4851 does), under-promotions must be counted separately, since =Q/=R/=B/=N lead to four different positions and hence four different continuations; so 12, not 3, is the right per-pawn factor.

(2) Piece multiset. Promotion means a side is not limited to 1 queen / 2 rooks / 2 bishops / 2 knights; up to 9 queens are possible. The script verifies a 9-ply legal game after which White already has 2 queens, so the "1*28" term is unjustified even in short reachable play.

(3) Consequently the total 132 is not an upper bound: the script computes exactly 218 legal moves in R6R/3Q4/1Q4Q1/4Q3/2Q4Q/Q4Q2/pp1Q4/kBNN1KB1 w (and 175 in a sparser 8-queen position), i.e. total_moves = 218 > 132 = claimed bound. Note that two of the claim's other constants are over-counts in the other direction (exhaustive 64-square sweeps give a bishop maximum of 13, not 14, and a queen maximum of 27, not 28), which does not help the bound; and the king factor 8 also ignores castling. The upper bound 132^4851 therefore does not follow — the correct per-position branching factor is at least 218 (218 is in fact the known maximum), so the argument's arithmetic base is wrong, though the qualitative conclusion (finitely many chess games) is unaffected: replacing 132 by 218 repairs the proof.

## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

Two ambulances at positions 0 and 1/2 (instead of the post's symmetric antipodal 0 and 1), in the exact stated model: incidents i.i.d. uniform on [0,1], response time = |incident - ambulance|, a dispatched ambulance is permanently unavailable, horizon of 2 incidents.

Stage-2 (last incident) values: leaving the ambulance at 1/2 behind costs int_0^1 |y-1/2| dy = 1/4; leaving the ambulance at 0 behind costs int_0^1 y dy = 1/2.

GREEDY ("send the closest car") dispatches the ambulance at 1/2 for every x > 1/4, so on x in (1/4, 3/8) it saves a small distance now and strands the fleet at the badly placed endpoint 0. Example pointwise losses (exact): x = 7/24 -> greedy total 17/24 vs optimal 13/24 (loss 1/6); x = 5/16 -> 11/16 vs 9/16 (loss 1/8); x = 1/3 -> 2/3 vs 7/12 (loss 1/12).

Exact expectations of TOTAL response time over the 2 incidents:
  E[greedy]  = 3/32 + 17/32 = 5/8   = 0.625
  E[optimal] = 21/128 + 57/128 = 39/64 = 0.609375
  gap = 1/64 > 0 (per-incident averages 5/16 vs 39/128).
The optimal stage-1 rule is "dispatch the ambulance at 0 iff x <= 3/8", differing from greedy's threshold 1/4 on a positive-measure set. Both policies agree at stage 2 (nearest is optimal with one incident left), so the entire gap comes from the stage-1 decision.

Largest gap found in the sweep: positions {0, 1/24, 2/3}, E[greedy] = 55/108 vs E[optimal] = 5178487/10616832, gap 228233/10616832 ~ 0.0215.

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **The proof concludes that the greedy "dispatch the nearest available ambulance" policy is globally optimal for minimizing expected average response time (and that its two-incident analysis "can be generalized to larger sizes"). This general claim is false: it holds only for the special symmetric 2:1 configuration analyzed (all ambulances sitting at one of two antipodal points 0 and 1), where the immediate-distance ordering happens to coincide with the ordering of "positional value". A tiny asymmetric instance in the exact same model (uniform incidents on [0,1], response time = distance, dispatched ambulance permanently unavailable, finite horizon of 2 incidents) makes greedy strictly suboptimal.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> Once the phone rings, sending the closest car is in fact globally optimal.

Context of the original problem:

> Title: Optimizing response times of an ambulance corp: short-term versus average
> 
> Background: I work for an Ambulance service. We are one of the largest ambulance services in the world. We have a dispatch system that will always send the closest ambulance to any emergency call. There is a belief that this results in the fastest response time as an average across the system.
> 
> Example: Suppose we have the following simplified scenario. We have 3 ambulances available (labelled A, B and C). At any given point in time, there is an random chance of an emergency call originating equally anywhere inside this box:
> 
> If an emergency job appears (labelled 1), we will send the closest ambulance (in this case Ambulance C)
> 
> You will notice that Ambulances A and B are very close together on the left side of the box (lets pretend they are just leaving a hospital after dropping off their patients). There  [...]

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The claim is a universally quantified optimality statement about a fully specified finite-horizon decision problem, so one rational ambulance configuration with an exactly computed expected-cost gap refutes it.

The script computes, in exact Fraction arithmetic with no floats anywhere in any comparison or reported quantity, the expected total response time of (a) the greedy nearest-available policy and (b) the true optimal policy, for every configuration in a bounded grid. Stage-2 value g(S) = int_0^1 min_{r in S} |y-r| dy is integrated in closed form by splitting [0,1] at the positions of S and the midpoints between consecutive positions, so the integrand is affine on each piece and the trapezoid rule is exact. Stage 1 integrates the lower envelope of the finitely many functions h_a(x) = |x-a| + g(S\{a}), splitting [0,1] at all kinks a and all pairwise crossings (rational, from solving s1(x-a1)+c1 = s2(x-a2)+c2 for both slope signs), again making each piece affine. Greedy is integrated with the selection rule argmin_a |x-a| over the position/midpoint partition. Greedy ties occur only on a finite set, so no expectation depends on the tie rule.

Result: 3303 of the 3315 examined configurations make greedy STRICTLY suboptimal, so the failure is generic rather than a knife-edge artifact. The simplest witness is the 2-ambulance configuration {0, 1/2} with exact gap 1/64.

NEGATIVE CONTROL (guards against a buggy comparator that flags everything): in the n=2 sweep over the grid of denominator 24, greedy is optimal on EXACTLY the 12 mirror-symmetric pairs {t, 1-t} -- 0&1, 1/24&23/24, ..., 11/24&13/24 -- and on no others. That is precisely the case in which both ambulances have identical positional value, so the immediate-distance ordering coincides with the future-value ordering, which is the exact structural explanation stated in the target claim; the search reproduces it independently. The symmetric antipodal configuration {0,1} analyzed in the post therefore correctly shows gap 0 (greedy = optimal = 3/4), confirming the post's own two-ambulance computation while showing its generalization fails.

INDEPENDENT VERIFICATION of the witness by a structurally different method: a certified exact Lipschitz Riemann sandwich on a uniform partition into M = 4096 cells (both integrands are 1-Lipschitz, so each cell contributes within w/2 of its endpoint values), all in Fractions. It yields E_greedy in [10480641/16777216, 10489855/16777216] and E_optimal in [2495/4096, 2497/4096]; these intervals are strictly separated with lo(greedy) > hi(optimal), and the closed-form values 5/8 and 39/64 lie inside their respective bounds.

Hand-checkable: E_greedy = int_0^{1/4}(x + 1/4)dx + int_{1/4}^1(|x-1/2| + 1/2)dx = 3/32 + 17/32 = 5/8; E_opt = int_0^{3/8}(x + 1/4)dx + int_{3/8}^1(|x-1/2| + 1/2)dx = 21/128 + 57/128 = 39/64 < 5/8.

Hence "sending the closest car is in fact globally optimal" is false as a general statement; it holds only in the symmetric configurations where positional values tie.

## Object

The certificate witness, as recorded by the triage stage:

Take any fourth-power n with d=n^{3/4}>=2; concretely n=16, d=8. In the construction, let one left vertex l1 choose r1 in all 8 draws. This is a valid sampling trace. After multiple edges are collapsed to a single edge, l1 has simple neighborhood {r1}, so its degree is 1, not 8. Thus exact left degree is not guaranteed by the construction.

## What it kills

The flawed step of QEDBench problem Algorithms_4, solution 5, reads:

> Every vertex in L has degree exactly n3/4 (by construction).

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its
conclusion, refuting the step **as written** (not necessarily the problem's
headline theorem — see the module docstring for scope).

## Why it works

From the Lean module docstring
(`lean/qedbench/ProofCerts/Algorithms/Alg4.lean`):

**Algorithms_4 (sol5) — sampling-with-replacement + collapse does NOT guarantee left degree d**

The candidate solution constructs a bipartite graph by random sampling and asserts:

> each left vertex picks `d = n^{3/4}` right neighbors **with replacement**, multi-edges
> are collapsed, and the resulting graph has every left vertex with (simple) degree
> **exactly** `d`.

This is false: sampling *with replacement* can repeat right vertices, and collapsing the
resulting multi-edges then leaves **fewer** than `d` distinct neighbors. "Degree exactly
`d`" is only guaranteed when all `d` draws are distinct, which no draw-with-replacement
trace is forced to satisfy.

**Concrete witness (`n = 16`, `d = n^{3/4} = 8`).** Consider one left vertex `l1` and the
sampling trace in which **all eight draws return the same right vertex `r1 = 0`**. Each
individual draw is a legal outcome of an independent uniform sample from the `16` right
vertices (the constant trace has probability `(1/16)^8 > 0`, so the construction does not
exclude it). After collapsing multi-edges, the simple neighborhood of `l1` is the single
vertex `{r1}`, so its simple degree is `1`, not `8`. Hence the claim "every left vertex
has simple degree exactly `d` " fails on this valid trace.

Numerically verified: `d^4 = 8^4 = 4096 = 16^3 = n^3` (so `d = n^{3/4}` exactly over the
integers); the constant trace is in range; the collapsed neighborhood is `{0}`; the
simple degree is `1 ≠ 8`.

**Modeling choices**
* Right vertices are `Fin 16`; the `d = 8` draws of the focal left vertex `l1` are a
  **trace** `t : Fin 8 → Fin 16` (draw `i` returns right vertex `t i`). Sampling *with
  replacement* means **every** such function is a possible outcome; the witness trace is
  the constant function `draws := fun _ => 0`.
* Validity of the trace is the (per-draw) range condition `(draws i).val < n`, checked
  for all `i : Fin 8` by `decide` — each draw individually is a legal uniform sample.
* Collapsing multi-edges: after collapse, `l1` is adjacent to `r` iff **some** draw hits
  `r`. `adjOf t r` spells this out as an explicit `Bool` disjunction over the eight draws
  (no `∃`, no folds), so it reduces in the kernel.
* The **simple degree** of `l1` is the explicit `Nat` sum over the sixteen right vertices
  of `(adjOf t r).toNat` (the `GT1` `degree` style — no `Finset.card`/`Finset.filter`),
  i.e. the number of *distinct* right neighbors after collapse.
* The flawed claim, specialized to the focal left vertex, is
  `Claim : ∀ t : Fin 8 → Fin 16, simpleDegreeOf t = d` — every sampling trace yields
  simple degree exactly `d`. We never ask `decide` to enumerate the function type
  `Fin 8 → Fin 16`: the refutation `claim_fails` instantiates the universal claim at the
  concrete trace `draws` and contradicts the kernel-checked fact
  `simpleDegreeOf draws = 1` (the `GT20` negation-unpacking style). All `decide` goals
  quantify over `Fin 8` / `Fin 16` only.

hits.body_md:
## Object

Fix an enumeration $(q_n)$ of $\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]$. For any $x \in [0,1]$, density of
the rationals lets one choose $n_1 < n_2 < \cdots$ with $|q_{n_k} - x| < 1/k$: every
$x$ is a subsequential limit. Conversely all terms lie in $[0,1]$, so no limit escapes.

## What it kills

The intuition that lim sup / lim inf capture the whole cluster structure, and that
"divergent" means "settling into finitely many phases". Between $\liminf = 0$ and
$\limsup = 1$, *everything* is attained along subsequences.

## Debugging uses

- Any proof that extracts "the" convergent subsequence and treats its limit as
  canonical: here different extraction rules give different limits, so downstream
  uniqueness claims need justification (e.g. via a separate uniqueness argument or by
  showing all limits agree).
- Stress case for algorithms that estimate limits from trailing windows of a stream:
  trailing averages of an enumeration of rationals converge or not depending on the
  enumeration order — ordering is a genuine degree of freedom, not a detail.
- Construction template: to realize any closed set C as the cluster set, interleave
  sequences converging to a countable dense subset of C.

## Remarks

Compare Cesàro: some enumerations have Cesàro mean → 1/2, others oscillate; summability
of a sequence with a continuum of cluster points is order-sensitive.
hits.counterexample: Any enumeration q_1, q_2, ... of Q ∩ [0,1] is a bounded sequence whose set of subsequential limits is all of [0,1] — an uncountable continuum of cluster points. More generally, the set of subsequential limits of a bounded sequence can be any nonempty closed subset of R.
hits.refutes: A bounded sequence has at most countably many subsequential limits; divergent bounded sequences oscillate between "a few" cluster values.
